THE BIRTH OF CALIFORNIA

A MODERN CREATION MYTH

by Stephen A. McNallen

Long ago, Odin called all the Gods and Goddesses together in council. As the benches of Valhalla filled, there was a buzz of speculation as to why the Father of the Gods should have summoned them all, but while many voiced the question, no lips responded with an answer.

When all were seated and the proper rites had been observed, Allfather rose, fixed his ice-blue eye on one after another of his kin, and finally spoke:

"I have looked deeply into the Well of Wyrd, and held long converse with Mimir's bodyless head, and felt the runes burning into my hand as I tossed them; the three spoke as one...We are to build a nursery."

Aesir and Vanir alike muttered and puzzled; was Frigga pregnant? Was there to be a birth in Asgard?

But Odin stilled them with a wave of his hand, and told them more. "It is not a God being born , nor yet one of humankind, nor any other wight in the Worlds, but rather a whole folk, a tribe destined to grow strong in Midgard. And it is in Midgard that the nursery, their home acres, their kingdom, must stand."

In words of magic cadence, speaking in rhyme and in kennings, he outlined his plan. When he finished, all was silent in the great hall, and Odin's night-black ravens floated from the rafters to perch on his chair. Then, as one, the Gods and Goddesses rose to begin the task directed by their ancient Sire.

Njord gave the land selected by Odin a long sea coast, and set the waves to lapping against it. The waters were made to teem with fish, and seals played in the surf while gulls wheeled overhead, from time to time skimming the brine and leaving their tracks in the sand.

Skadi covered the high mountains with a coat of snow, and dropped wolves into the powder, rolling and shaking the white dust from their fur. Howling, they ran in circles as she sped down the slopes on her skis. Down the hills she went, to Njord's shore and back again, creasing the cleft of the rivers in her passing.

Freya was so moved by the new land that she wept for the beauty of it all, and the dwarves collected her golden tears and hid them away, deep inside the mountains, where they would one day be prized by the folk who would live here.

Frey and Sif together fashioned a wide valley and made its soil rich for the growing of all kinds of fruits and vegetables, and for the raising of livestock. The dark earth and the sand layered itself deep at their command, and they braided it with the rivers to nourish the crops.

Odin himself painted the sky a deep blue, to urge the new folk to rise above the concerns of the everyday, and to extend the reach of their minds and spirits. This was to be a place that encouraged the new and bold, a nursery that opened onto the wondrous universe.

But when they were almost done at their craft, waves tall as the hills rose from the sea and threw themselves against the land. Roaring over the rocks and trees, the furious waters threatened to destroy all the handiwork of the Gods and Goddesses. Valleys were flooded and mountains were scoured. Birds squawked and circled aimlessly. Fish flopped in the snow of Skadi's peaks.

It was Heimdal who spied the cause, and bellowed for the one who could set things right - mighty Thor. For the cause of all this evil was none other than the Midgard serpent, submerged off the coast. Thor rattled to the rescue, vaulted over the railing of his chariot, and had his hammer in his hand before you could say "Jormundgandr!" Wading into the waves, he kept an eye open for his foe - then struck, again and again! But no matter how strong his blows, the water got in the way and he could not connect with the coiling and roiling snake.

At length, tiring, he thought of another way to beat the worm. Heaping up rocks from the mountains and dirt from the great valley, he piled them higher and higher on top of the world-girdling serpent, forming yet another range of mountains right along the coast. Soon the monster was pinned beneath the weight. Thor rinsed his hands in the water and soon was gone, but the ground still shakes on occasion even today, as the world serpent tries to free itself.

Soon the Gods had cleaned up the mud, reestablished the shoreline, and things were peaceful once more. Odin stood high on a hill to the north of a great bay and stared with his one eye, looking far out to sea. Slowly, he spoke, and the sound of his voice was like the rumbling of the surf:

"From every corner of the Northlands, our sons and daughters will come to this fair place. They will have forgotten us, except as legend and as a dream almost unremembered in the night. But from them will come some who will know us again, and they shall grow to be a mighty folk. When their fellows are weak, they will be strong. They will show the way to all those descended from our loins, that the path to Valhalla will again be known."

As he raised his spear, a rainbow appeared at his feet, and Odin led all the Gods and Goddesses back to Asaheim. But they linger near the land they made for us, and often we can feel them in the snow and sea, the light, and land.

DRENGSKAPR

STEPHEN A. MCNALLEN

Christ's disciples wanted to know how to pray, and their master gave them the Lord's Prayer. Asatruar, on the other hand, want to know how to live - and the answer from Asgard is not a prayer for the bended knee, but rather a code for the fearless and fair: drengskapr, in the ancient tongue of the Northlands.

To understand this concept, we have first to grasp the root word from which it springs. A dreng was a gallant lad, a young man who was a member of a warrior band or some other relatively small group where one had to be able to depend on others for livelihood or even for life itself. The ship's crew, the merchant guild, the military unit - all these were examples of this tightly knit in-group. From the nature of these bands, we can infer a lot about what drengskapr must have been in the days of our ancestors, and what it must be to us today.

The dreng must be strong and courageous, but that pretty much goes without saying. These were expected during the Viking Age. Beyond bravery, there were other traits, most of which seem to revolve around how the individual related to the others in the group. Honesty, even to the point of bluntness, was preferred because in the war band or the ship's crew there was no place for hidden animosities that might boil over at a crucial moment and bring disaster to all. Likewise, a certain cheerfulness or at least a stoic acceptance of hardship helped to maintain morale when times were tough - when the group's endeavors were not prospering, when the ship had to be hauled over long portages, or when rations were short. Generosity, always admired in Norse society, was even more important for the dreng. One who shared with his fellows - a meal, a knife, a bowstring - furthered the survival of all.

All of these characteristics spring from the dynamic of small teams surrounded with threats to their safety and success. The idea of drengskapr uses these very practical survival traits as a springboard to a larger nobility, a highness of mind, the opposite of all that is lowly or niggardly or petty. It is in open opposition to the viking stereotype of a cruel, blood-soaked savage with no moral code. True, not every viking followed the high standards of the dreng, but the ideal was there, and all could aspire to it.

Drengskapr implies certain duties to a friend, but also to a foe. The Germanic tribesmen amazed the Roman soldiers by picking them up and dusting them off after a skirmish. Today, we might well consider this as going too far; the survival of the group has to be considered. But it does raise the question of just what we owe our enemies.

The Christians say we should love our enemies, and this is where they go wrong. We don't owe them love - but we owe them respect in the measure they deserve it. The valor and skill of our foes does us honor, and we should honor them in return.

In the mainstream culture which surrounds us, drengskapr is rare. You can find vestiges of it in the football team and the Army unit, but in general we live in a world that has turned its back on noble conduct. Its widespread revival may have to await tougher times, when the exigencies that called it into being are once more a part of daily life. And it may be that drengskapr was always for a special group, an adventurous elite. But who can deny that our world needs this model of fairness, generosity, and bravery? And where can it start, if not with us, as we go about our lives each day?
